title: Update to my game engine's tooling: Radial Menu, better mesh carving
author: Sencha-Games
selftext:
It's been a while since my last post! I've been making less visible progress on the engine lately, mostly optimizing the renderer, cleaning up technical debt, adding multiplayer, gameplay frameworks and other stuff that's really cool but isn't much to show off. 

I've been furious lately about modern UI design, so this past weekend I started thinking of ways to make my game engine's UI more pleasant to look at and use. Metalheart inspired theme + radial menu is doing a lot for my enjoyment of using the tool. 

I've also added arches and ngon support to my carve tool. This is import because it will allow me to create windows and doorways in a matter of seconds. Not shown in the video are a clipping tool (works the same way it does in Hammer) and a modifier stack (currently only has Array and Mirror mods)

I think I'm about 70% of the way there to "Version 1.0" of my engine! The big features that are still left are animation controllers and full ability kit and level flow integration with the scripting API, which would allow gameplay logic to be orchestrated with flowcharts (higher level than UE's blueprints, used for queries and high-level verbs). After that, it's a matter of sanding out rough edges and working on deployment pipelines.  
  
The flagship title I intend on making with this is a first person Metroidvania with a 90s cyberspace and body horror aesthetic. I won't say much about it, but it's heavily inspired by David Bowie's Outside Album. Hopefully I'll be posting progress on that game by the end of the year! 

Here is a link to the engine's repo:  
[https://github.com/GavynBryan/Sencha](https://github.com/GavynBryan/Sencha)

comments.author: thewowcollector
comments.body: Wait you built an engine? How was that process?

replies.author: Sencha-Games
replies.body:
Yes! I've been working on it for about 8 months. 

It started off as a dependency injection container and a collection of common services for building games. Then I outgrew that concept and started making the engine more concrete and opinionated. 

Forcing those separations early, though, I think was helpful for Claude to build the Vulkan renderer, since it could be split into granular services with their own loggers and explicit dependencies, it was much easier to debug when things went wrong. 

I think I started on this project with Claude Opus 4.5. With increasingly more intelligent models coming out, my involvement has progressively gotten higher level and more focused on user experience rather than micromanaging implementation details.
